quote_item6: The videos were evaluated by three urologists using two validated questionnaires: Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT) and DISCERN (quality criteria for consumer health information), classifying them according to the score of the latter, in poor quality (1–2 points) and moderate/good quality (3–5 points).

Items 1-3 HIGH: single Spanish-language keyword search on 9 March 2021, first 50 videos sorted by views, filtered to 38. Item9 HIGH: single-day search, no observation window. quote_item6: To this end, we use the NewsGuard database (8). As of 2022 March, NewsGuard indexes 6860 English and 145 German language domains. Each domain is scored on a scale of 0 (very poor) to 100 (exceptional quality journalism) points. Domains with less than 60 points are considered “not trustworthy” (8).
quote_item10: After excluding links to social media websites and search engines, the database covers 46.5% of links posted by members of the US Congress and 58.8% and 39.2% of links posted by members of the German and British parliament, respectively.
notes: Methodologically the strongest study in the shard: near-census of a real, enumerable population (1023 US handles = 61.7% of members of the 114th-117th Congress; 65.7% DE, 78.6% UK), full behavioural trace 2016-01-01 to 2022-03-16 via Twitter API, external professional domain list (NewsGuard) plus a robustness check against an independently compiled list. Item6 LOW under the instrument's ‘validated domain/credibility list’ clause, though the NewsGuard standard is credibility/transparency rather than falsity. Item10 HIGH relative to an audience-level prevalence claim: the denominator is NewsGuard-rated links only (46.5% of US links) posted by political elites, not any audience's whole information diet. 3,200-tweet-per-account scrape cap noted; authors report a supplementary all-tweets analysis with no appreciable difference.

Items1-2 HIGH: the universe is a vaccine/COVID keyword-seeded corpus, so the population is a curated topical one. Item10 HIGH: the 2.7% denominator is URL-bearing topical tweets, not any audience's whole diet, and messages are the unit rather than people.

quote_item6: For misinformation, respondents were asked to indicate whether or not they encountered misinformation during the pandemic, where they came across such information and how often, on a Likert scale from one to five, they found themselves involved in misinformation.
quote_item10: The majority of respondents 269/295 (91.2%) claimed to have come across misinformation during the pandemic.
notes: Item10 LOW and item1 LOW: this is one of the few person-denominated estimates in the shard (269/295 real respondents), and the target population (Moroccan university students) is a real audience, not an artefact of the measurement. Everything upstream is weak: item2/3 HIGH (questionnaire pushed to ‘various faculties and online student groups’, self-selected, no sampling frame), item4 HIGH (no response rate; 303 received, 295 retained, denominator of invitees unknown), item6 HIGH (misinformation is whatever the respondent labels as such; author categorisation of the volunteered examples is topical, not a falsity verification), item7 HIGH (instrument ‘validated’ only by a 10-person pilot, no psychometrics), item9 HIGH (recall window is the unbounded ‘during the pandemic’). Six affirmative HIGHs give HIGH overall even though the load-bearing item10 is LOW.
